analysis.one_liner: Widened estate tax exemption and cut rate for large inherited fortunes and farm property.
analysis.headline: No cosponsors joined; the bill never left the Senate Finance Committee and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cut the estate tax. The tax applies only to estates above a certain size—roughly the top 1% of estates. The bill raises the exempt amount to $5 million per person and drops the top rate from 45% to a flat 35%. It also adds generous breaks for inherited farms and family businesses, and makes several tax cuts permanent instead of expiring in 2010.
analysis.who_benefits: Very wealthy families and owners of large farms and businesses. The estate tax already only applies to a small share of estates, so nearly all benefit flows to heirs of multi-million-dollar estates.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the estate tax exemption to $5 million per person, indexed to inflation.
Replaces the graduated rate structure with a flat 35% rate.
Increases the special-use valuation reduction for inherited farms and businesses from $750,000 to $5 million.
Raises the family-owned business deduction cap to $2.5 million and makes it permanent.
Repeals the sunset on the 2001 tax cuts' estate and gift tax provisions.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government (general taxpayers), who lose estate tax revenue; future beneficiaries of federal programs funded by general revenue, and to a lesser extent public services funded by Congress, which would face tighter budgets.

drawbacks.text: Cuts revenue from one of the most progressive parts of the tax code; the burden falls entirely on large estates.
Repealing the sunset locks in the tax cut permanently, adding to long-term deficits.
The $5 million farm and business valuation reduction is far larger than most working farms, so the break mostly helps the largest agricultural operations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Gives a large, permanent tax cut concentrated in the top 1% of estates, at the cost of federal revenue. No offsetting revenue provision is included, so the cost would be borrowed.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with no cosponsors and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up; it died at the end of the 109th Congress.

narrative.text: Introduced June 29, 2006 by Sen. Mary Landrieu.
Referred to the Committee on Finance on the day of introduction; no further action was taken.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large estates kept the existing estate tax rules; the proposed tax cut was never enacted, and federal revenue was not reduced by this bill.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors and no floor action, so no vote or partisan breakdown exists.

industries.industry: Large family-owned farms and agricultural operations
industries.note: Would have allowed a $5 million valuation reduction for inherited farm property, sharply reducing estate tax on large farm heirs.
Deduction cap raised to $2.5 million and made permanent, sheltering business interests from estate tax.
Higher exemption, lower flat rate, and permanent extension reduce the estate tax entirely for many large estates and reduce demand-shaping for estate-planning services.
